# Shrinkage Methods

<h2> Ridge regression </h2>
<h2> Scaling of predictors </h2>
<h2> The lasso and variable selection </h2>
<h2> Choosing $\lambda$ by cross-validation </h2>
<h2> The "loss + penalty" framework </h2>

::: notes
- Based on ISLR Section 6.2. We implement ridge in closed form and the lasso by coordinate descent so that glmnet is no longer a black box.
:::

## Shrinkage Methods: Ridge Regression and Lasso

- Subset selection fits least squares on a *subset* of the predictors.
- Alternative: fit a model with **all** $p$ predictors using a technique that *constrains* or *regularizes* the coefficients, i.e., **shrinks** them toward zero.
- Shrinking the coefficient estimates can significantly reduce their variance.

Recall least squares minimizes
$$
\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p\beta_jx_{ij}\Big)^2.
$$

## Ridge Regression

$$
\hat\bbeta^R_\lambda = \argmin_{\bbeta}\;\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p\beta_jx_{ij}\Big)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2 = \text{RSS} + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2
$$

- $\lambda\ge0$ is a **tuning parameter**; $\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2$ is the **shrinkage penalty** (the intercept is not penalized).
- $\lambda = 0$: least squares. $\lambda\to\infty$: all $\beta_j\to 0$.
- Closed form (centered $\by$, standardized $\bX$):

$$
\hat\bbeta^R_\lambda = (\bX^\T\bX + \lambda\bI)^{-1}\bX^\T\by
$$

::: fact
$\bX^\T\bX + \lambda\bI$ is invertible for every $\lambda > 0$, even when $p > n$ or the predictors are collinear.
:::

## Ridge from Scratch: Credit Data

```{r}
library(ISLR2)
y <- Credit$Balance
X <- model.matrix(Balance ~ ., data = Credit)[, -1]
n <- nrow(X)
Xs <- scale(X) * sqrt(n / (n - 1))           # standardize with divisor n
yc <- y - mean(y)
ridge <- function(lambda) solve(crossprod(Xs) + lambda * diag(ncol(Xs)), crossprod(Xs, yc))
lambdas <- 10^seq(-2, 5, length = 100)
B <- sapply(lambdas, ridge)
rownames(B) <- colnames(X)
round(B[c("Income", "Limit", "Rating", "StudentYes"), c(1, 50, 100)], 2)
```

## Ridge Coefficient Paths

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.4
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hl <- c("Income", "Limit", "Rating", "StudentYes")
cols <- ifelse(rownames(B) %in% hl, c("black", "red", "blue", "orange")[match(rownames(B), hl)], "gray80")
matplot(lambdas, t(B), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = cols, log = "x",
        xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "Standardized coefficients")
legend("topright", hl, col = c("black", "red", "blue", "orange"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
ratio <- apply(B, 2, function(b) sqrt(sum(b^2))) / sqrt(sum(B[, 1]^2))
matplot(ratio, t(B), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = cols,
        xlab = expression(paste("||", hat(beta)[lambda]^R, "||"[2], " / ||", hat(beta), "||"[2])), ylab = "")
```

- Left: each curve is one predictor's coefficient as a function of $\lambda$. Right: the same, indexed by $\|\hat\bbeta^R_\lambda\|_2/\|\hat\bbeta\|_2$.

## Ridge Regression: Scaling of Predictors

- Least squares estimates are **scale equivariant**: multiplying $X_j$ by $c$ scales $\hat\beta_j$ by $1/c$.
- Ridge estimates can change **substantially** when a predictor is rescaled, because of the penalty $\sum_j\beta_j^2$.
- Therefore, standardize the predictors first:

$$
\tilde x_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij}}{\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2}}
$$

```{r}
X2 <- Xs; X2[, "Income"] <- X2[, "Income"] * 1000            # income in dollars, not $1000s
r1 <- solve(crossprod(Xs) + 50 * diag(11), crossprod(Xs, yc))["Income", ]
r2 <- solve(crossprod(X2) + 50 * diag(11), crossprod(X2, yc))["Income", ] * 1000
c(standardized = r1, rescaled = r2)     # not the same fit!
```

## Why Does Ridge Help? Bias-Variance Trade-off

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.38
set.seed(4750); ns <- 50; p <- 45; beta <- rnorm(p, sd = 0.4)
Xsim <- matrix(rnorm(ns * p), ns); Xtest <- matrix(rnorm(500 * p), 500)
ftest <- Xtest %*% beta
lam <- 10^seq(-2, 3, length = 30)
fits <- replicate(100, {
  ysim <- Xsim %*% beta + rnorm(ns)
  sapply(lam, function(l) Xtest %*% solve(crossprod(Xsim) + l * diag(p), crossprod(Xsim, ysim)))
}, simplify = "array")                       # 500 x 30 x 100
bias2 <- colMeans((apply(fits, c(1, 2), mean) - as.vector(ftest))^2)
variance <- colMeans(apply(fits, c(1, 2), var))
matplot(lam, cbind(bias2, variance, bias2 + variance), type = "l", lwd = 3, lty = 1, log = "x",
        col = c("black", "#2E8B57", "#C2185B"), xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "")
legend("top", c("squared bias", "variance", "MSE"), col = c("black", "#2E8B57", "#C2185B"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
```

::: notes
- With p = 45 close to n = 50, least squares has huge variance. Ridge trades a little bias for a large reduction in variance.
:::

## The Lasso

- Ridge always includes **all** $p$ predictors in the final model; it cannot select variables.
- The **lasso** minimizes

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p\beta_jx_{ij}\Big)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^p|\beta_j| = \text{RSS} + \lambda\|\bbeta\|_1
$$

- The $\ell_1$ penalty forces some coefficients to be **exactly zero** when $\lambda$ is large enough $\Rightarrow$ **variable selection**, **sparse** models.
- As with ridge, choosing $\lambda$ is critical: cross-validation.

## Lasso by Coordinate Descent

Minimizing over one coordinate $\beta_j$ with the others fixed has a closed-form **soft-thresholding** solution

$$
\beta_j \leftarrow \frac{S\!\left(\sum_i x_{ij}r_{ij},\ \lambda/2\right)}{\sum_i x_{ij}^2},\qquad S(z,\gamma) = \text{sign}(z)(|z|-\gamma)_+ ,
$$

where $r_{ij} = y_i - \sum_{k\neq j}x_{ik}\beta_k$ is the partial residual. Cycle over $j$ until convergence.

```{r}
soft <- function(z, g) sign(z) * pmax(abs(z) - g, 0)
lasso_cd <- function(X, y, lambda, beta = rep(0, ncol(X)), tol = 1e-4, maxit = 1e4) {
  r <- as.vector(y - X %*% beta); xx <- colSums(X^2)
  for (it in 1:maxit) {
    old <- beta
    for (j in seq_along(beta)) {
      r <- r + X[, j] * beta[j]                       # partial residual
      beta[j] <- soft(sum(X[, j] * r), lambda / 2) / xx[j]
      r <- r - X[, j] * beta[j]
    }
    if (max(abs(beta - old)) < tol) break
  }
  beta
}
```

## Lasso Coefficient Paths: Credit Data

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.4
lamL <- 10^seq(5, 0, length = 80); b <- rep(0, ncol(Xs)); BL <- matrix(NA, ncol(Xs), length(lamL))
for (k in seq_along(lamL)) BL[, k] <- b <- lasso_cd(Xs, yc, lamL[k], beta = b)   # warm starts
rownames(BL) <- colnames(X)
matplot(lamL, t(BL), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = cols, log = "x",
        xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "Standardized coefficients")
legend("topright", hl, col = c("black", "red", "blue", "orange"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
apply(BL[, c(20, 40, 60)], 2, function(b) names(which(b != 0)))
```

## Comparison with `glmnet`

```{r}
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE)
library(glmnet)
# glmnet minimizes RSS/(2n) + lambda * penalty, so lambda_glmnet = lambda / (2n)
g <- glmnet(Xs, yc, alpha = 1, lambda = 1000 / (2 * nrow(Xs)), standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE,
            thresh = 1e-14)
cbind(ours = lasso_cd(Xs, yc, 1000, tol = 1e-10, maxit = 1e6), glmnet = as.numeric(coef(g))[-1]) |> round(3)
```

## Choosing $\lambda$ by Cross-Validation

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.38
set.seed(4750)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(Xs))); lamCV <- 10^seq(4, 0, length = 20)
cv_err <- rowMeans(sapply(1:5, function(k) {
  tr <- folds != k; mx <- colMeans(Xs[tr, ]); my <- mean(yc[tr])
  Xtr <- sweep(Xs[tr, ], 2, mx); Xte <- sweep(Xs[!tr, ], 2, mx); b <- rep(0, ncol(Xs))
  sapply(lamCV, function(l) {                       # warm starts along the path
    b <<- lasso_cd(Xtr, yc[tr] - my, l, beta = b)
    mean((yc[!tr] - my - Xte %*% b)^2)
  })
}))
plot(lamCV, cv_err, log = "x", type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#003366",
     xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "5-fold CV error")
abline(v = lamCV[which.min(cv_err)], lty = 2, col = "red")
```

::: tip
In practice: `cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)` does this (with the "one-standard-error" rule as an option). We study cross-validation in Chapter 8.
:::

## The Variable Selection Property of the Lasso

Why does the lasso, unlike ridge, give coefficients that are **exactly** zero? Equivalent constrained problems:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Lasso:** $\displaystyle\min_{\bbeta}\ \text{RSS}\quad\text{s.t.}\ \sum_{j=1}^p|\beta_j|\le s$
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Ridge:** $\displaystyle\min_{\bbeta}\ \text{RSS}\quad\text{s.t.}\ \sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2\le s$
:::
::::

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.36
#| echo: false
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
g1 <- seq(-1.5, 3, length = 200)
rssq <- outer(g1, g1, function(a, b) 1.2 * (a - 1.7)^2 + 1.6 * (b - 1.2)^2 - 1.8 * (a - 1.7) * (b - 1.2))
for (type in c("Lasso", "Ridge")) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(-1.5, 3), ylim = c(-1.5, 3), asp = 1, axes = FALSE, main = type,
       xlab = "", ylab = "")
  arrows(-1.5, 0, 3, 0, length = .1); arrows(0, -1.5, 0, 3, length = .1)
  text(2.9, -0.2, expression(beta[1])); text(-0.25, 2.9, expression(beta[2]))
  if (type == "Lasso") polygon(c(1, 0, -1, 0), c(0, 1, 0, -1), col = "cyan", border = NA)
  else symbols(0, 0, circles = 1, inches = FALSE, add = TRUE, bg = "cyan", fg = NA)
  contour(g1, g1, rssq, levels = c(0.3, 1, 1.9), add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
  points(1.7, 1.2, pch = 19); text(1.85, 1.35, expression(hat(beta)))
}
```

The RSS ellipses first touch the $\ell_1$ diamond at a **corner** (some $\beta_j = 0$); the $\ell_2$ disk has no corners.

## Flexibility of the "Loss + Penalty" Framework

$$
\text{Minimize}\ \ \color{blue}{\text{Loss}} + \lambda\,\color{red}{\text{Penalty}}
$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
lp <- data.frame(
  Loss = c("Hinge: $\\sum_i[1-y_if(\\mathbf x_i)]_+$", "Squared error: $\\sum_i(y_i - f(\\mathbf x_i))^2$",
           "Squared error", "Squared error", "Hinge", "Negative log-likelihood"),
  Penalty = c("$\\lambda\\|\\mathbf w\\|_2^2$", "$\\lambda\\|\\mathbf w\\|_2^2$", "$\\lambda\\|\\mathbf w\\|_1$",
              "$\\lambda_1\\|\\mathbf w\\|_1 + \\lambda_2\\|\\mathbf w\\|_2^2$", "$\\lambda\\|\\mathbf w\\|_1$",
              "$\\lambda\\|\\mathbf w\\|_1$"),
  Algorithm = c("SVM", "Ridge regression", "Lasso", "Elastic net", "1-norm SVM", "Penalized logistic regression"))
knitr::kable(lp, escape = FALSE)
```

## Summary

::: instructions
- Ridge: $\ell_2$ penalty, closed form $(\bX^\T\bX+\lambda\bI)^{-1}\bX^\T\by$, shrinks but keeps all predictors.
- Lasso: $\ell_1$ penalty, soft-thresholding by coordinate descent, produces sparse models.
- Standardize predictors before penalizing.
- Tune $\lambda$ by cross-validation; penalization trades bias for variance.
:::

Modify `lasso_cd()` to fit the **elastic net** $\text{RSS} + \lambda[\alpha\|\bbeta\|_1 + (1-\alpha)\|\bbeta\|_2^2]$. (Hint: the update becomes $S(\cdot)/(1 + \cdots)$.)
:::
